Pathophysiology
Crohn’s Disease and Ulcerative Colitis  ​Crohn’s disease may 
involve any part of the GIT, but approximately 50% to 60% of cases 
involve the distal ileum and the colon. Only the small intestine or 
only the colon is involved in 15% to 25% of cases. Disease activ-
ity in UC is limited to the large intestine and rectum. In Crohn’s 
disease, segments of inflamed bowel may be separated by 
healthy segments, whereas in UC the disease process is continu-
ous (see Figure 28-3). Mucosal involvement in Crohn’s disease 
is transmural in that it affects all layers of the mucosa; in UC the 
disease normally is limited to the mucosa. Crohn’s disease is 
characterized by abscesses, fistulas, fibrosis, submucosal thick-
ening, localized strictures, narrowed segments of bowel, and 
partial or complete obstruction of the intestinal lumen. Bleed-
ing is more common in UC (see Table 28-4).
